text: I’ll model the fluid as the union of the 120 mm × 200 mm chamber and four horizontal rectangular prisms. I interpret “40 mm above the floor” as the **bottom edge** of each 30 mm-high port (so each port spans z = 40–70 mm), and “15 degrees off tangent” as a 15° inward radial component from the local tangent. Each 50 mm duct runs from its inlet plane to the cylindrical-wall intersection along that axis. I’ll first make and inspect this coarse solid in metres.

The first inspection exposed an important issue before meshing: `Cylinder` defaults to axial centering, placing the floor at −0.1 m. I’ll rebuild it explicitly bottom-aligned at z = 0 and render using the available off-screen backend without the unavailable Xvfb helper.

The coarse view confirms the intended tangential arrangement and a single connected fluid solid. Next I’ll inspect the exact boundary faces after the Boolean union so patch assignment follows face provenance and orientation—not bounding-box guesses. The top disk will then be partitioned into the 40 mm outlet and the remaining top annulus.

The union has 27 boundary faces: one cylindrical wall, floor, top, four inlet planes, and five exposed wall pieces per duct. I’ll now create the requested nine wall/opening groups, splitting the original top face exactly into a 40 mm disk and annulus, and export each group as its own STL. I’ll also verify patch areas and that all patches together reproduce the complete boundary area.

All 12 requested patch STLs are exported (four inlets, outlet, cylinder wall, floor, top, and four separately named duct walls), and their summed area exactly matches the original solid boundary. I’ll now create a coarse 5 mm Cartesian background mesh around the geometry; `snappyHexMesh` will retain the connected interior containing the chamber centre.
This OpenFOAM build does not accept `blockMesh -overwrite`; no mesh was written. I’ll rerun the same dictionary with the supported plain invocation.

The background mesh is correct at 5 mm resolution (70,400 cells). I’ll now snap it to the twelve STL regions, with one additional surface-refinement level (nominal 2.5 mm near boundaries) so the 20 mm-wide ports and 40 mm outlet are represented cleanly while remaining a coarse first mesh.

`snappyHexMesh` requires minimal `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` files even though no flow solution will be run. I’ll add only those mesh-utility dictionaries, recreate the snappy dictionary in this successful step for reproducibility, and rerun.

The snapped coarse mesh completed with 51,360 cells and no mesher-level quality errors. I’ll now run the binding `checkMesh` test and inspect the final boundary patch table to confirm that every requested patch survived with nonzero faces.

The all-geometry check identified 1,361 concave polyhedral cells, so I will not accept the snapped mesh even though its ordinary metrics are good. I’m switching the volume meshing stage to Gmsh tetrahedra, using the same exact STEP fluid solid and the same named STL patch geometry. First I’ll import the STEP into Gmsh and imprint the outlet disk onto the top face, then inspect the resulting CAD face inventory before meshing.

The imprint operation preserves the single fluid volume and creates exact outlet (0.00125664 m²) and top-annulus (0.01005310 m²) boundary faces; the unsplit original top is only an orphan CAD face and will be excluded by querying the volume boundary. I’ll now assign physical groups directly from those exact boundary faces, generate a 4 mm tetrahedral mesh, and convert it to OpenFOAM.

The tetrahedral trial revealed that exporting the face-only imprint to STEP did not carry the split into the volume boundary: Gmsh correctly reported zero outlet faces, so this mesh is not acceptable. I’ll redo the imprint as a volume–surface Boolean fragment (rather than fragmenting only the top face) and verify that both the outlet disk and annular top are actual faces of the single volume boundary.

The corrected Boolean now yields one volume with 28 boundary faces, including the exact outlet disk and top annulus. I’ll remesh this corrected volume and require every physical patch group—including the outlet—to contain at least one CAD face before conversion.

The corrected conversion now contains all twelve requested patches, including the outlet. I’ll run full topology and geometry checks on this tetrahedral mesh and inspect patch face counts; any nonzero `defaultFaces` patch would indicate an unassigned boundary and will be rejected.

The final tetrahedral mesh passes all full `checkMesh` checks: 150,398 cells, 12 nonempty named patches, no default patch, maximum non-orthogonality 50.3°, and maximum skewness 0.609. I’ll make one final visual inspection of the converted OpenFOAM mesh surface and compare its total volume against the CAD fluid volume.

Final verification shows the OpenFOAM mesh volume differs from the exact CAD volume by only 0.0475%, and the surface view confirms all four angled ducts and the closed vessel shape.

Built in metres:
- Chamber: measured 0.120 m internal diameter × 0.200 m height.
- Outlet: measured 0.040 m diameter.
- Four ports: 0.020 m wide × 0.030 m tall.
- Duct axes: measured 15.000° off each local tangent; length 0.050 m.
- Port vertical placement: assumed “40 mm above the floor” means the **bottom edge** is at z = 0.040 m (top at z = 0.070 m).
- Final mesh: 150,398 tetrahedra; 12 nonempty requested patches; full `checkMesh -allGeometry -allTopology` reports `Mesh OK`.
- One STL per patch is in `constant/triSurface`.
- No flow solution or boundary conditions were created.
- No requested property was left unchecked.

The advisory surface checks found that independently tessellating the CAD faces caused nonconformal STL edge sampling at patch seams (184 welded free edges) and triangle crossings near Boolean junctions. The volume mesh itself is valid, so I’ll replace each STL with the corresponding conformal final boundary triangulation. This preserves the same exact patch geometry while guaranteeing shared seam vertices and consistent, noncrossing facets.

The replacement STLs now use the conformal boundary triangles from the checked mesh; open edges reported per individual patch are expected patch perimeters, while the welded union should be closed. I’ll rerun completion checks without waivers.
